title: What time is it?
goal: Read and say the time in two systems, make an appointment, and ask questions in three different ways.
bekal: tell the time with *il est … heures*
tell conversational time from official 24-hour time
ask questions with intonation, with *est-ce que*, and with inversion
wave: Go back to **Unit 5** first: describe your own family from memory — who they are, how old they are, where they live.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — On se donne rendez-vous
dialogs.intro: Camille and Budi set a time to meet and study together.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Il est dix heures et quart.
lines.literal: it is ten hours and quarter.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Déjà ? Le cours commence à onze heures.
lines.literal: already? the course begins at eleven hours.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: On a le temps. Il finit à quelle heure ?
lines.id: We have time. What time does it end?
lines.literal: one has the time. it finishes at which hour?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: À midi et demi. Tu es libre cet après-midi ?
lines.id: At half past twelve. Are you free this afternoon?
lines.literal: at midday and half. you are free this after-midday?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oui. Est-ce que tu veux réviser ensemble ?
lines.id: Yes. Do you want to study together?
lines.literal: yes. is-it-that you want review together?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Avec plaisir. À quatorze heures à la bibliothèque ?
lines.id: I'd love to. At 2:00 at the library?
lines.literal: with pleasure. at fourteen hours at the library?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Quatorze heures, donc deux heures de l'après-midi.
lines.id: Fourteen hundred, so two in the afternoon.
lines.literal: fourteen hours, so two hours of the after-midday.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Voilà. Ne sois pas en retard !
lines.literal: there-it-is. not be not in lateness!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je suis toujours à l'heure, moi !
lines.literal: I am always at the-hour, me!

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Ah bon ? Hier tu es arrivé à midi moins dix.
lines.id: Oh really? Yesterday you showed up at ten to twelve.
lines.literal: ah good? yesterday you are arrived at midday minus ten.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Le bus, encore le bus. Ce n'est pas ma faute !
lines.id: The bus, the bus again. It's not my fault!
lines.literal: the bus, again the bus. it not-is not my fault!

notes: **Il est … heures**, and the word *heures* can't be dropped. *Il est dix* on its own means nothing. Compare English, where "it's ten" is enough.

**Il here doesn't refer to anyone.** Just like *il y a*, this is an empty *il*, there only to carry the verb — exactly like English "it" in "it's ten o'clock". The weather verbs in Unit 18 use the same *il*.
**Une heure is singular, deux heures plural.** *Il est une heure* (one o'clock), *il est deux heures* (two o'clock). The s in *heures* is silent, but you still have to write it.
**Midi and minuit don't take heures.** *Il est midi* (noon), *il est minuit* (midnight). Both are masculine, so the half hour is *midi et demi*, not *demie*.
**Et quart, et demie, moins le quart.** Quarter past, half past, quarter to. Notice that *demie* agrees with feminine *heure* — except after *midi* and *minuit*.

**Official time uses the 24-hour clock.** Train timetables, movie times and formal appointments always say *quatorze heures*, *dix-neuf heures trente*. In everyday conversation people use the 12-hour clock and add *du matin*, *de l'après-midi*, *du soir* — like a.m. and p.m.
**Ne sois pas** is the negative command form of *être*. Commands are covered in full in Unit 17; for now just recognize *ne sois pas en retard* as one whole chunk.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Two systems living side by side. The conversational one is used between friends; the 24-hour one is used for anything written.
after: ⚠️ *Moins* counts back from the **next** hour: 8:45 is not "eight forty-five" but "nine minus a quarter". English does the same with "a quarter to nine", so this one is actually easy.
To ask when something happens, use **à**: *à quelle heure ?* — *à huit heures*. Don't mix it up with *quelle heure est-il ?*, which asks the time right now.
Time-of-day helpers: *du matin* (in the morning, until about 11), *de l'après-midi* (in the afternoon), *du soir* (in the evening), *de la nuit* (late at night).

grammars.title: Three ways to ask a question
body: French has three levels of formality for the same question. All are correct; only the setting differs.
after: *Est-ce que* has no meaning of its own at all — it just signals that a question is coming, a bit like English "do" in "do you come?". It's said ehs-kuh, and before a vowel it becomes *est-ce qu'* (*est-ce qu'il vient ?*).
Inversion slips in a **-t-** when two vowels collide: *a-t-il ?*, *va-t-elle ?*, *parle-t-on ?* That t is there purely for the sound.
When in doubt, use *est-ce que*. It's right in any setting and never changes the word order.

blocks.text: To tell the time you only need up to 60. The numbers above that have surprises of their own and are saved for Unit 9.

blocks.title: Number sound traps
items: *Six* and *dix* on their own are said SEES and DEES. Before a noun starting with a consonant, the last letter goes silent: *six livres* (see LEEVR). Before a vowel it becomes a z sound: *dix ans* (dee-ZAHN).
*Neuf* is said NUHF, but before *ans* and *heures* the f turns into a v: *neuf ans* (nuh-VAHN), *neuf heures* (nuh-VUHR). Only those two words.
*Huit* is said WEET, and its h blocks liaison: *les huit livres* (lay WEE LEEVR), not lay-ZWEET.
*Vingt* on its own is said VAN, but from 21 to 29 the t wakes up: *vingt-deux* (vant-DUH).

blocks.text: The numbers 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61 slip in **et** with no hyphen: *vingt et un*, *trente et un*. The others use a hyphen: *vingt-deux*, *trente-trois*.

exercises.prompt: Write the time out in words, conversational style.
Turn these into questions with est-ce que.

answers: Il est sept heures. — Il est neuf heures et quart. — Il est onze heures et demie. — Il est deux heures moins le quart. — Il est sept heures moins dix. — Il est minuit.
Est-ce que tu viens ce soir ? — Est-ce qu'il travaille le samedi ? — Est-ce que vous parlez français ? — Est-ce qu'elle habite à Lyon ? — Est-ce que nous commençons à huit heures ?
Quelle heure est-il ? — Il est dix heures et quart. — Le cours commence à onze heures. — Tu es libre cet après-midi ? — Ne sois pas en retard !
